content: 1. The Omsk hemorrhagic fever virus is a pathogen that requires specific handling and containment measures, particularly when cultured in laboratory settings. 2. Poliovirus, when cultured, must be managed under strict biosafety protocols to prevent accidental exposure or environmental release. 3. Rabies virus, in its cultured form, necessitates stringent containment to mitigate risks associated with its high pathogenicity. 4. Rickettsia prowazekii, a bacterium cultured for research or diagnostic purposes, demands careful handling due to its potential to cause epidemic typhus. 5. Rickettsia rickettsii, the causative agent of Rocky Mountain spotted fever, requires specialized containment when cultured to ensure safety. 6. Rift Valley fever virus, a zoonotic pathogen, must be cultured under high biosafety conditions to prevent transmission to humans or animals. 7. The Russian spring-summer encephalitis virus, a tick-borne pathogen, requires strict containment during culturing to avoid accidental exposure. 8. Sabia virus, a member of the arenavirus family, is highly pathogenic and must be handled with extreme caution in laboratory settings. 9. Shigella dysenteriae type 1, when cultured, necessitates rigorous containment to prevent outbreaks of severe dysentery. 10. Tick-borne encephalitis virus, a neurotropic pathogen, requires specialized containment during culturing to prevent accidental transmission. 11. Variola virus, the causative agent of smallpox, is subject to the highest level of biosafety containment due to its eradicated status and potential use as a bioterrorism agent. 12. Venezuelan equine encephalitis virus, a mosquito-borne pathogen, must be cultured under strict biosafety conditions to prevent accidental release. 13. West Nile virus, a flavivirus, requires careful handling during culturing to mitigate risks of laboratory-acquired infections. 14. Yellow fever virus, a mosquito-borne flavivirus, must be cultured under stringent containment to prevent accidental exposure. 15. Yersinia pestis, the bacterium responsible for plague, requires high-level biosafety containment when cultured to prevent accidental release or exposure. 16. African swine fever virus, a highly contagious pathogen affecting pigs, must be cultured under strict containment to prevent agricultural outbreaks. 17. Avian paramyxovirus Type 1, specifically the velogenic Newcastle disease virus, requires specialized containment during culturing to prevent transmission to poultry. 18. Classical swine fever virus, a significant pathogen in pigs, must be cultured under strict biosafety conditions to prevent agricultural and economic impacts. 19. Foot-and-mouth disease virus, a highly contagious pathogen affecting livestock, requires the highest level of containment during culturing. 20. Goatpox virus, a pathogen affecting goats, must be cultured under strict biosafety protocols to prevent outbreaks. 21. Lumpy skin disease virus, a pathogen affecting cattle, requires specialized containment during culturing to prevent transmission. 22. Mycoplasma mycoides, the causative agent of contagious bovine pleuropneumonia, must be cultured under strict biosafety conditions. 23. Peste des petits ruminants virus, a pathogen affecting small ruminants, requires careful handling during culturing to prevent outbreaks. 24. Rinderpest virus, an eradicated pathogen, must be cultured under the highest biosafety conditions due to its historical significance and potential risks. 25. Sheep-pox virus, a pathogen affecting sheep, requires specialized containment during culturing to prevent transmission. 26. Swine vesicular disease virus, a pathogen affecting pigs, must be cultured under strict biosafety protocols to prevent agricultural impacts. 27. Vesicular stomatitis virus, a pathogen affecting livestock, requires careful handling during culturing to prevent accidental exposure. 28. Infectious substances affecting animals, such as those listed above, must be transported under strict packing instructions to ensure safety and containment. 29. Packing Instruction P620 applies to the transport of infectious substances classified under UN 2814 and UN 2900. It mandates the use of leakproof primary and secondary receptacles, absorbent materials, and rigid outer packaging to prevent leakage and ensure containment. 30. Packing Instruction P650 applies to the transport of biological substances classified under UN 3373. It requires packaging to withstand shocks, vibrations, and environmental changes during transport, with at least three components: a primary receptacle, secondary packaging, and rigid outer packaging. 31. For substances transported with refrigerants like dry ice or liquid nitrogen, the packaging must maintain integrity at low temperatures and allow for the safe release of gases to prevent pressure buildup. 32. Infectious substances must be labeled and marked appropriately, with clear visibility of required information, including the proper shipping name and UN number. 33. When dry ice is used as a refrigerant, the packaging must allow for the release of carbon dioxide gas to prevent pressure buildup. The shipper must provide documentation detailing the quantity of dry ice and ensure compliance with ventilation safety procedures. 34. Infectious substances must be transported in a manner that ensures they arrive at their destination in good condition, without posing a hazard to humans or animals. 35. Empty packaging that previously contained infectious substances must be disinfected or sterilized before reuse, and any labels indicating the presence of infectious substances must be removed or obliterated.
